messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Khin was a 41-year-old South Eastern Asian man who had come to treatment after months of feeling as though he was no longer moving through his life in a stable way. Before the trauma, he had built a life around dance, discipline, and routine, and he and his wife had settled into the ordinary rhythms of marriage with the predictability he had once valued. That steadiness was shattered while he was working as a relief worker in a war zone, where one afternoon he found himself moving through streets marked by smoke, shattered buildings, and the metallic, acrid smell of something burned. The attack he witnessed and the desperate work that followed were recorded in his mind with painful clarity. He spoke of being on duty at the same time of day the event had occurred, and of how the light outside his window now seemed to carry the same weight it had then, making that hour feel loaded before anything even happened.

In the aftermath, Khin found that reminders arrived without warning and with a force that startled him. A smell of alcohol on another person’s breath, the odor of a bottle opening nearby, or even a faint burnt smell from food in the kitchen could instantly pull him back into the scene. He described how these cues did not simply make him think about what happened; they dropped him into it. He would be standing in the hallway at home or passing through a rehearsal space, and suddenly the room around him would seem to fall away. What was in front of him became less real than the memory, and he felt as if the frightening event were happening again in the present tense, with the same urgency and bodily alarm it had carried before. He did not experience these moments as ordinary recollections. They came on with no warning, and he often felt caught in them before he could make sense of what had been set off.

Khin was especially troubled by the shame that flooded him when the memory surfaced. He said that when he remembered the event, he felt intense shame, not only because of what he had seen but because of what he believed he had become in that setting. He was preoccupied with the sense that he had acted in ways that went against who he was. As he spoke, it was clear that this was not a passing regret but a settled, painful judgment about himself. He had come to believe that his reactions since the event showed he was a lousy coper, the sort of man who should have been able to keep himself together and could not. He was equally fixed on the conviction that he could not rely on himself. That belief showed up in the way he described everyday moments: once he noticed a smell or the time of day lined up with the trauma, he no longer trusted what he would feel, how long it would last, or whether he would manage to stay grounded.

Over time, these experiences began to spill into his daily life. As a dancer, Khin could not avoid studios, changing rooms, performance venues, and the bodies and breath of other people, so reminders found him in the middle of ordinary professional moments. A faint alcohol smell from a colleague after an evening gathering, or a burnt odor from a backstage appliance, could leave him abruptly distant and unsettled. He became more watchful about the time of day and increasingly wary of places where those smells might appear. Although he kept working, he found himself carrying a private burden into rehearsals and home life, measuring himself against the person he had once believed himself to be. He and his wife had noticed that he was less easy in the evenings, more preoccupied when the same hour returned, and less confident in his own judgment.

By the time he sought help, Khin was not asking only for relief from the memories, but for some way to feel like himself again. He was frightened by how quickly his surroundings could seize him and how completely the scene could return. More than anything, he feared the possibility that he could not trust his own mind or reactions, and he hoped treatment might help him recover a sense of steadiness without having to brace for the next sudden return of the war into his present life.
